lines.title: hook
lines.text: A database does not scan a table to find a key. It keeps keys sorted in pages and jumps. Here is a trick: if every page is sorted, and each page starts above where the last one ended, then the whole set of pages is a single sorted array folded into rows.

lines.title: one sorted array
lines.text: Five pages of six keys. Read them left to right, top to bottom, and it is thirty sorted keys. So binary search works, as long as we can turn a flat position into a page and a slot.

lines.title: the translation
lines.text: The translation is one line: page equals position divided by six, slot equals the remainder. We are looking for thirty-seven. The middle position is fourteen, which is page two, slot two. Its key, sixty-one, is above thirty-seven, so the upper half is gone. The new middle is six: page one, slot zero, key twenty-seven, below thirty-seven, so the lower half is gone.

lines.title: converging
lines.text: Middle ten: page one, slot four, key forty-four, too high again. Middle eight: page one, slot two, key thirty-seven. Found, in four probes out of thirty keys. Real engines usually search the page boundaries first and then inside the page. Flattening is the same arithmetic in a single search.

lines.title: facts
lines.text: Twenty probes find one key among a million, since log base two of a million is about nineteen point nine. Four probes here. And one line of arithmetic, divide and remainder, connects the flat index to the page.
